sections.h2: Is there a separate city tax bill in Lexington?
sections.html:
No. Lexington and Fayette County operate as one government, the Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government (LFUCG), which replaced the separate city and county governments in the early 1970s. The Fayette County Sheriff collects property tax for the whole territory, and the Fayette County PVA values every parcel. The total bill is built from rates set by the Commonwealth, the LFUCG, Fayette County Public Schools and a few other districts.

What differs from one address to the next is the service district. Seven residential districts appear on the PVA's 2026 chart, and each pays the same base lines for state, schools, general services, the extension office, soil conservation, public health, Lextran buses and parks. Only the curbside extras separate them.

sections.h2: Service districts and what they add
sections.html:
Curbside charges by Lexington service district, per $100 of assessed value
Service districtAdded charge
Full service (trash pickup, street lights, street cleaning)17.3 cents
Refuse only13.7 cents
Street lights only2.7 cents

Combinations fall in between. The school line is the biggest piece of every bill at 79.7 cents per $100, about 63 percent of the full-service total of $1.2598. Find the district number on your bill or ask the PVA, because it changes what a buyer will pay each month.

Two surcharges apply only in certain places. When the LFUCG Vacant Property Review Commission labels a parcel abandoned and blighted, the owner pays $1 more per $100 of taxable value, which makes a neglected vacant house expensive to hold. A parcel inside the Downtown Lexington Management District pays an extra 10 cents per $100.

Owners of empty houses should learn whether the commission has certified theirs before listing. The LFUCG can tell you, and a buyer will price the surcharge into any offer.

Lexington was the first American city to adopt an urban growth boundary, in 1958. Inside it, in the urban service area, development can proceed at city density. Outside, in the rural service area, parcels had to be at least 40 acres, a rule meant to shield the horse farms around town. The boundary was widened in 1996 by 5,300 acres.

For a seller, the line decides which kind of parcel you have. Property outside it can sit on a large lot in farm use, and Kentucky assesses farmland at agricultural value instead of market value, which changes the tax math completely. Pull the parcel record from the PVA to confirm the tax district and land use before pricing. Expect different answers for a subdivision lot inside the line and for acreage outside it.

Lexington is Kentucky's second-largest metro, and the city itself held 322,570 people in 2020, with an estimate of 329,751 for 2025. The consolidated city spans 285.5 square miles. Since 1990 each decade has added between 9 and 16 percent. Fayette County Public Schools runs six district high schools, 12 middle schools and 37 elementary schools, so the school line on your bill is the same wherever the house sits. I-75 skirts the city and I-64 runs along the north, and Blue Grass Airport is on the west side.

Once a bill is delinquent, the Fayette County Clerk is the office to deal with, and its rules are rigid. A delinquent bill is a lien, so the clerk wants certified funds. Interest raises the balance each month.

  • Accepted: cash, a money order, or a cashier's or certified check payable to the Fayette County Clerk.
  • Turned away: personal checks, business checks, counter checks and credit cards.
  • Not available: partial payments on a delinquent bill.

Owners who cannot pay in full can phone the Fayette County Attorney's Office at 859-254-4941 to ask about a payment arrangement.

Visit Room 132 at 162 E. Main Street, Lexington, KY 40507, or call 859-253-3344 during payoff hours of 8:00 to 4:30. The clerk's deeds website has a search tool and a calculator. Each year the clerk sells eligible delinquent bills to third-party purchasers between 90 and 135 days after the sheriff's handoff. A seller should obtain the payoff before the listing goes live.

sections.h2: Transfer tax and property tax at closing
sections.html:
Selling a house here triggers the state transfer tax in KRS 142.050: $0.50 for each $500 of price, with any leftover fraction counted as a full unit. The grantor bears it, and the Fayette County Clerk computes it and collects before the deed can be filed. Foreclosure transfers, transfers between spouses in a divorce, and parent-to-child transfers for nominal consideration are exempt.

Property tax runs on a separate track. Whoever held title at the start of the year gets the bill, and the contract or settlement statement says how the cost is divided. A seller who is 65 or disabled may be receiving the $49,100 homestead exemption in force for 2025 and 2026, but a buyer must file a new application with the Fayette County PVA.

Every residential bill is built from the same base lines: state, schools, general services, the extension office, soil conservation, public health, Lextran buses and parks. The service district adds the curbside lines on top. If two neighbors on different streets pay different totals, the district is almost always the reason, and the district number is printed on the bill.

When you list, a buyer will ask what the house costs to carry. Print the bill, circle the district and have the figure ready. A house in a district without trash pickup or street lights will show a lower total, and a buyer who sees the reason will not read it as an error. If the number on the bill looks wrong for your address, call the PVA before you advertise it. The PVA can confirm the district and the assessed value in a single call.

sections.h2: Steps before you list a Lexington house
sections.html:
Pull the parcel record from the PVA and confirm the service district, the assessed value and whether any exemption is on file. Ask the sheriff for the current bill. If anything is delinquent, get a payoff from the Fayette County Clerk at Room 132, remembering that only certified funds are accepted there, and give the figure to your closing agent.

If the house is vacant, ask the LFUCG whether the Vacant Property Review Commission has certified it as abandoned and blighted, since the extra $1 per $100 comes with it. A cash sale can skip a buyer's lender and its appraisal timeline, but the tax bill, the transfer tax and any lien are settled the same way at closing.

faqs.q: Is there a separate city property tax in Lexington?
faqs.a: No. Lexington and Fayette County share one urban county government, so the single bill from the Fayette County Sheriff covers state, school, county and urban-government charges. Rates depend on the service district of your address.

faqs.q: What is the biggest part of a Lexington tax bill?
faqs.a: The school line. On the PVA's 2026 chart it is 79.7 cents per $100 in each residential district, set against a full-service total of $1.2598.

faqs.q: How much extra does a blighted Lexington property pay?
faqs.a: An extra $1 per $100 of taxable value once the LFUCG Vacant Property Review Commission certifies it as abandoned and blighted.

faqs.q: Can I pay delinquent Lexington tax with a credit card?
faqs.a: No. The Fayette County Clerk takes only cash, money orders and cashier's or certified checks for delinquent bills, and it does not accept partial payments.

faqs.q: What is the Lexington transfer tax on a home sale?
faqs.a: Under KRS 142.050 the seller pays $0.50 per $500 of price at recording, collected by the Fayette County Clerk.
